subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES
speechtext: On Friday, February 13, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) inquired about the nature of representations made by Canada concerning United States import restrictions on dairy products. As indicated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) on February 11, the Canadian government has now made official representations to the United States government on three occasions. The United States government replied to the first of these representations that it was seeking the repeal of the legislation.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES
speechtext: What date was that?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES
speechtext:
That was the first one indicated in the appendix to Hansard. These restrictions were discussed also during the 1951 and 1952 sessions of the contracting parties to the general agreement on tariffs and trade. In order to give a detailed explanation of the nature of the Canadian representation, I should like to make the following statement:
The United States import restrictions on dairy products were originally instituted on 68108-1271
August 9, 1951, in accordance with an amendment of July 31, 1951, to the Defence Production Act. This amendment, which was written into section 104 of the act, required the imposition of controls over fats and oils, butter, cheese and other dairy products, if the importation would:
(1)	Impair or reduce domestic production;
(2)	Interfere with orderly domestic storing or marketing;
(3)	Result in any unnecessary burden or expenditure under any government price support program.
The Canadian government had followed with deep concern the discussions in the United States congress when this amendment to the Defence Production Act was introduced. These discussions indicated that there was a substantial volume of opinion which was opposed to this amendment and which was aware that its adoption and application would be contrary to United States international obligations. When the amendment was passed, the Canadian government deemed it appropriate to protest officially against this legislation. Accordingly a note was presented to the state department by the Canadian embassy in Washington on August 27, 1951-that is the date the hon. member was inquiring about- which pointed out that these restrictions were contrary to the obligations of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
Efforts were made by the United States administration, and by various individual members of the United States congress, to obtain repeal of these restrictions. The president asked congress on August 23, 1951, for prompt repeal of the restrictions. On September 22, 1951, the United States state department replied to our note drawing attention to efforts then being made by the president to obtain repeal of the restrictions and stating that it understood the concern of the Canadian government.
These restrictions were discussed at the September-October 1951 meeting of the contracting parties to the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
A resolution adopted on October 26, 1951, which was supported by the Canadian delegation, found the restrictions to be an infringement of the agreement. The resolution took note of the United States government's intention to seek remedial legislation.

Inquiries of the Ministry
Subsequently on January 17, 1952, a second note to the United States state department drew the attention of the United States government to the proceedings at the session of the contracting parties to the general agreement on tariffs and trade and urged the United States government to remove the restrictions without further delay. At that same time there was a bill before the United States senate for repeal of the restrictions. However, this bill failed to pass.
When the United States Defence Production Act was amended in June, 1952, modifications were made to section 104 which permitted some degree of liberalization. The Secretary of Agriculture was authorized to set quotas by types and varieties and to permit additional imports of each type and variety up to 15 per cent of the import limitation. Under authority of this legislation the import controls have been relaxed from time to time.
The contracting parties to the general agreement on tariffs and trade again considered these restrictions at their session in September-October, 1952. A resolution was adopted, which was supported by the Canadian delegation, and which noted that the United States had not repealed these restrictions and indicated that the contracting parties should be free, if they deemed it appropriate, to take retaliatory action after prior consultation with other contracting parties.
On December 30, 1952, the United States government, acting under the mandatory provisions of section 104 of the United States Defence Production Act, imposed import quotas on dried whole milk, dried buttermilk, and dried cream. The Canadian government again examined the situation arising from this legislation and took the occasion to present a third note drawing attention to the general effects of these measures on the broad commercial policy interests of both governments and urging the removal of the restrictions as soon as possible.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES

I thank the Prime
Minister for his statement and I should like to ask one question arising out of it. Is there any prospect of these unfairnesses against Canadian dairy products being removed or at least relaxed by the United States government?

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STRIKE OF GRAIN HANDLERS, VANCOUVER AND NEW WESTMINSTER
speechtext:
I
should like to address a question to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour. Does he care to make a statement with regard to the strike of the grain handlers in the cities of Vancouver and New Westminster? This work stoppage has wide ramifications.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. Cote (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: STRIKE OF GRAIN HANDLERS, VANCOUVER AND NEW WESTMINSTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
thank the hon. member for giving notice of this question which has to do with the dispute and strike affecting local 333, International Union of United Brewery, Flour, Cereal, Soft
Inquiries of the Ministry Drink and Distillery Workers of America, and various Vancouver grain elevator companies.
The following is a brief review of events leading up to the present situation involving the previously mentioned parties.
The collective agreement between the parties was entered into on May 30, 1952, effective December 1, 1951, until November 30, 1952; and thereafter to remain in effect unless written notice is given by either party to the other at least thirty days prior to November 30, 1952, that revision of the agreement is desired.
Such notice was given on October 28, 1952, by the union to (1) Searle Co. Ltd.; (2) Pacific Elevators Ltd.; (3) United Grain Growers Ltd.; (4) Kerr Gifford and Co. Inc.; and (5) Alberta Wheat Pool, all of Vancouver, B.C.
The main proposals included:	(1) the
eight-hour five-day week, starting midnight Sunday and ending midnight Friday; (2) a 10 cent premium for employees working on the third or midnight shift; (3) three extra statutory holidays; (4) three weeks' vacation after 10 years' service; (5) that the new agreement contain a list of job classifications; (6) 12 cents per hour increase in present rates; and (7) dust money of 10 cents per hour.
Representatives of both parties held meetings in November, 1952, but could come to no agreement. On November 17, 1952, the situation was discussed by Mr. Edward Sims, Canadian director of the union and Mr. R. H. Tupper, Q.C., representing the companies, with our senior conciliation officer at Vancouver, Mr. George Currie. Both parties expressed the opinion that further negotiations either with or without the assistance of the conciliation officer would be useless and stated the parties desired the establishment of a board of conciliation.
On November 21, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) received a joint request for the establishment of a board of conciliation and investigation to deal with the dispute, and on November 22 a board was established. The companies nominated Mr. Thomas E. H. Ellis, and Mr. James Bury was nominated by the union. In the absence of a joint recommendation by these nominees of the parties the minister on December 18 appointed Dr. Joseph A. Crumb, professor of economics and political science, University of British Columbia, to be the third member and chairman of the board.
On January 23, the minister received the report of the board making the following recommendations:	One, the work day and
2000	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry the work week; that the employers undertake to minimize Saturday and Sunday work but that they should not be committed to a standard Monday through Friday schedule for a work week. Two, premium for night shift; for the third shift the majority report recommended a differential of 10 cents per hour. The company nominee felt that existing arrangements were satisfactory. Three, statutory holidays; the majority report recommended that the number of holidays be fixed at eight. The company nominee recommended that the number be left at six. Four, vacations; that this request be set aside. Five, job classifications; the majority report recommended that this request be met but with the proviso that the union respects management's right to establish job classifications and to set rates applicable thereto. The company nominee disagreed. Six, wage rates; the majority report recommended that the present hourly rate of $1.50 should continue during the next contract year. The union nominee recommended that the 12-cent-per-hour increase be granted. Seven, dust premium; the majority report recommended a 10-cent-per-hour premium rate. The company nominee recommended that the existing uniform rate be maintained.
On January 29 the minister was informed that the recommendations of the board were not acceptable to the companies. On February 5, he was informed that the union accepted the majority recommendations signed by Dr. Crumb and Mr. Bury and the minority recommendation respecting wages signed by Mr. Bury.
On February 10, the Department of Labour was informed by the union that unless settlement was reached the employees would strike on February 16. Our information is that work stopped yesterday morning and operations are at a standstill. The total number of men involved is approximately 250. Both parties are aware, through an informal meeting with our conciliation officer on February 6, 1953, that mediation services of the department are available to them, but no request has been made by either party for further mediation. The department is constantly in touch with the situation and hon. members may be assured that everything possible will be done to bring about an early settlement of the strike.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO MOVE GRAIN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hardly think it can be said that the government is losing millions of bushels of sales. subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night I was attempting to deal with points that had been raised in the course of this debate which has now extended over some days. Last night I indicated that, though we had listened to many very interesting speeches, so far as the official opposition was concerned the proposals they had made on external affairs were characterized particularly by their vagueness.
When the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) was speaking last night he was asked what his own views were on these matters, and his reply-as it is reported at page 1988 of Hansard-which I suppose might serve as a guidepost for the views of members of the official opposition on foreign affairs, was
as follows:
I have just said that I believe Canada, in concert with other nations of the commonwealth and, in so far as it is possible, with the United States of America, should adopt a foreign policy which would carry not the hot war but the cold war to the communists, and keep them guessing for a change.
That might be considered rather vague as a direction in foreign policy. But there was not very much vagueness about the satisfaction of the official opposition over what was termed by more than one of their members the new policy of the United States in Asia. According to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), that new United States policy was to seize the initiative and, to quote his words, "to call the tune".
The same idea was referred to by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), when he talked about the stiffening of United States policy. And the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) used this expression, "a firm and positive policy", which, he thought, would bring peace. Firmness is of course a desirable attribute of policy. But I know hon. members will agree that firmness should not be confused with rashness, and it should not I suggest go beyond our strength. There is a good deal to be said, in the conduct of
External Affairs
international affairs, for using the velvet glove over the iron hand; but there is very little to be said in diplomacy for putting the iron glove over the velvet hand. The hon. member for Peel, when discussing this matter, gave an example of what he considered to be wise firmness in the conduct of foreign affairs. His example, and it was repeated by other speakers, was the Berlin airlift. But I would remind the house that the firmness displayed in the Berlin airlift was a firmness based upon realism, and applied very cautiously.
At the time of the blockade of Berlin there were many advocates of a firmer policy than that of the airlift, which took some time to be put into effect; that kind of firmer policy would have tried to defeat the blockade at once by running trucks across the border and by running trains into Berlin.
The kind of firmness which is based upon caution, and a clear assessment of our strength, is to be desired.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

The other kind of firmness is probably to be deplored. It is clear from the discussion we have had on foreign policy that members of the official opposition and of the Social Credit group welcome this new policy of firmness, while the members of the C.C.F. group leave no doubt as to where they stand. They view it with suspicion and in some of its manifestations they reject it.
So far as the attitude of the government is concerned, I think our views have been pretty clearly and carefully expressed and possibly can be best understood if I explain the attitude which we take toward some of the particular manifestations of the policy. It is easy to talk in generalities, especially when you are in the opposition; it is not so easy to talk in particularities, especially when you are in the government.
Let us take a few of these concrete matters on which we may have to express our views in the future. I took a few last night, but I shall add one or two this afternoon.
We have felt and we still feel, for instance, that Korea is a matter for the United Nations and that any action in which we participate in Korea or in connection with matters arising out of Korea would have to be as a result of a United Nations decision and not a national decision by any one participant in that action.
Similarly, I think we have made it quite clear that we would be opposed to- any decision or to any action which might extend the war in Korea unless there were pretty

External Affairs
convincing evidence that that action would also end the war. The extension of the war, to which I have just referred, seems on the other hand to have almost been welcomed by some of the speakers who contributed to this debate, and I am thinking particularly of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) and the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson).

speechtext: May I just correct the minister on that. I did not at any stage suggest an extension of the war. What I did suggest, and I think the minister will recognize it, was that a definite policy be adopted as quickly as possible by the United Nations for terminating the war.

It was my view then-
He indicated that it was still his view.
-that the military effort of the United Nations should not be limited to the country in which the aggression takes place.
He then went on to explain what he meant by that. It was on that statement that I based my observation.

an extension of the war to suggest that when an aggressor has been named by the United Nations every effort should be made to disarm the aggressor so that he cannot hit you any further?

That may be my hon.
friend's interpretation of what he said, and of course I accept his interpretation. But my own interpretation, which I think would be the same as that of many people who read that sentence and the remarks following, was that he meant it might be necessary to extend the war beyond Korea into China- and indeed he went further than China- in order to win it. I would suggest to the hon. member that he have another good look. at his speech.

I ask the minister if he can
take anything more from what I said than

that the only suggestion I made in connection with China was that the United Nations would certainly be justified in blockading the coast of China in order to keep war materials from going in which they would then throw back at our boys.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext:
I have read from the hon.
gentleman's speech. If I had the time I would be glad to read the subsequent paragraphs. We must agree to differ on the interpretation of what he said.
Then there is another very practical question, whether a stronger military offensive should be taken within the present strategy in Korea. The government's attitude toward that is that any such military action, even within the present strategy, should certainly be closely related to the political and military results which might follow from that action. I apologize to the hon. gentleman for referring to his speech once again, but I think I am quoting him accurately-in referring to the military situation some time ago, he said that in 1951-I believe he was referring to September-we had the communists on the ropes but the Far Eastern command refused to allow a knockout.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I was quoting General Van Fleet who said that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Just to keep the record straight on this, because these are very important matters and what we say in respect of them will go far beyond these four walls, may I say that at that time the Far Eastern command was the Far Eastern command of the United States under generals who were senior to General Van Fleet. The Far Eastern command in turn got its directions from the unified command, which was the chiefs of staff in Washington. So any military action which was taken at that time or not taken at that time was in accordance with the orders of the supreme military direction of that operation, which was in Washington and under General Bradley.
Lest there be any misunderstanding of the influence of civilian authority at that time, either national or international, it should also be made quite clear-because there has certainly been some misunderstanding lately on this matter-that when the decision was taken in 1951 to initiate armistice negotiations with the communists those negotiations were not meant to interfere with and did not necessarily interfere with the military operations which continued.
The hon. gentleman made special mention of General MacArthur's inability to bomb the Manchurian bases and asserted that that prohibition came from United Nations officials. I would be most interested indeed if he could

supply any evidence which would support the inportant allegation that United Nations officials would not allow General MacArthur to bomb Manchurian bases at any time since the Korean aggression commenced.
There is another practical question arising out of these Far Eastern discussions, on which government policy has already been indicated but which I shall repeat clearly this afternoon. I refer to the question of the blockade which has been very much in people's minds at the present time. Our attitude is that whether a blockade should or should not be imposed against the aggressor is a matter for United Nations decision. It is of course to be distinguished from action taken to prevent strategic materials going to the aggressor because action of that kind has been taken already on the part of the United Nations.
I would think myself that the only excuse for extending our action and imposing a naval blockade on the coast of China would be that it would be effective in ending the war. There is certainly a strong division of opinion on that subject, especially when it is realized that at least 75 per cent-various figures have been given'-of the supplies going to communist China to enable them to participate in this Korean aggression go by land rather than by sea. There would be dangers in the imposition of such a blockade; and before any action is taken they should be weighed very carefully against the effect of that blockade on the ending of the war. I can say that, so far as we are concerned, we would think in default of evidence to the contrary that the dangers and the difficulties would neutralize the beneficial effect which might result from such a blockade.
Then there is another question-and I mention this too to meet the criticism that I have been talking mincingly and in generalities. I am dealing with concrete matters which are not dealt with by some of the members across the aisle.

speechtext:
This is the question of
whether it would be wise to bomb Chinese communist territory incidentally to the Korean operation. Our policy is that that would be unwise unless such bombing were forced on the United Nations by all-out war from China itself.
I would point out to hon. members that we have not yet in Korea-and I mean by "we" the United Nations-been exposed to that kind of all-out war. Therefore we should be pretty careful, and it is generally agreed by military authorities that we should G8108-128i
External Affairs
be careful, in considering whether we should bomb Chinese territory.
There is another question which was dealt with by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie) in his interesting contribution to the house, as to whether or not it would be wise or unwise to take any action which would assist the forces of Chiang Kai-shek to secure a foothold on the mainland. There again, the policy of this government is to be very careful before we intervene to assist the nationalist government on Formosa in returning to China; because from past evidence we believe that-and again I have made some study of this matter as have other hon. members-the government which is now on Formosa did not reach Formosa because of a lack of support from outside or because it was betrayed, but that it reached Formosa because it was driven out of China.
We would probably not be very wise, from the point of view of defeating aggression in Korea, and possibly from other points of view as well if we identified our cause as members of the United Nations with the restoration of the nationalist government on Formosa to the mainland.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I mention these matters because they are problems which we may have to face. I do not, in mentioning them, suggest that we have any reason to assume that the decision which was taken in Washington a short time ago regarding Formosa means that any of these things is likely to be put forward by the United States or any other government. I do not think that these problems necessarily follow on the decision taken on Formosa. I am satisfied that that is not likely to be the case. I indicated last evening that I have had some assurance recently that these consequences of the Formosa decision are not likely to follow, and I hope that they will not.
Now, there is just one other statement from the official opposition with which I should like to deal for a short time because it was a very important one, which I am sure will cause a great deal of comment. That statement was contained in the speech the other evening by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson). He was certainly forthright enough in stating his own view. He attacked what has been called the "policy of containment", although I must confess that the word "containment" and the policy that it represents have been very often misunderstood. He attacked that policy very strongly and preferred what I think might fairly be described-although he did not use the words in this way-as "a dynamic liberation policy".

External Affairs
In his statement-and I do not want to do him any injustice-which appears on page 1900 of Hansard, he supported and advocated unlimited war. He said, and I quote from Hansard:
To pretend that we can prepare for and fight a limited war against a major power is nonsense.
He said, in another part of his speech:
It is only in men's minds that we think in terms of a limited war. This is now being changed in the United States.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, with all respect to the hon. member, that that is bad history; and that some of the most successful national wars in history have been successful because they have been limited, and some of the greatest catastrophes and failures in history have happened because leaders of nations who have led those nations into war did not recognize any limit to their objectives in war. If you want an example in terms of one country to explain what I mean, I would have you contrast Bismarck's policy of limited war with Hitler's policy of unlimited war. So, I am not at all prepared to believe that in Korea at this time we have to indulge in unlimited war, irrespective of where that may take us.
The hon. gentleman said it would also be desirable for us to lead from strength, and that there was no such thing as a safe war. He said that one of the things about the Formosa decision which gave him satisfaction was that it represented a step in the right direction. He went even farther than that and on page 1901 of Hansard he suggested that one of the things we might do now would be to destroy the Hong Kong-Shanghai railway. He advocated the imposition of a naval blockade-and he is not alone in that-and he advocated a positive policy of liberation of people behind the iron curtain. There has been a great deal of discussion about that lately, and he went on at page 1902 of Hansard to say that a policy of isolated war would not do that. He followed up that remark by saying:
Are we going to encourage an attack there on the flank?
In answering his own question he said:
Of course we are.
And then:
Why, then, should we not encourage an attack on the other flank in China?
That certainly, Mr. Speaker, is dynamic enough and I would like to say at once that no one on this side of the house could support that kind of dynamic, unlimited aggressive policy under the present circumstances. It will be very interesting for the

governments of Greece, Turkey and Yugoslavia to read that a member of our parliament has advocated that kind of action on our part.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I cannot wind up this debate without saying a few words about the Pacific security pact.

speechtext: Before the minister goes on, I would like to reply to him. I have never advocated military attacks. What I advocated is the same kind of action as the communists are taking now. I may say that my view is that we are not dealing with tulips; we are fighting communism. In destroying poison ivy it is better to wear boots than ballet shoes.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think, in view of what the hon. member has said, I should just quote from Hansard so that there will be no misunderstanding. If I have misrepresented the meaning of his words I shall be glad to withdraw the interpretation that I gave them, but I will just read what he said. This appears at page 1902 of Hansard:
A policy of restricted action, of containment, of an Isolated war is something that does not bring them encouragement.
He refers there to the people behind the iron curtain who are looking for liberation. That-
-policy . . . does not bring them encouragement.
He is talking about an isolated war.
They want to be free; they want to get out from under the yoke of communism. Just as we are fighting communism, so they want to fight communism.
In the next paragraph he discussed the recent political developments in the Balkans which have led to the association of Greece, Turkey and Yugoslavia. He went on to say:
I am sure that the impact of this anti-cominform pact on countries like Bulgaria, Albania and even Roumania is certainly very considerable. Now, are we going to encourage that? Are we going to encourage an attack there on the flank? Of course we are. Why, then, should we not encourage an attack on the other flank in China? There are many ways of beating the communists, and we have to use all of them.
Those were his words, and the house will of course be able to draw its own conclusions from them.
I should like now to make a few comments about a Pacific security pact. In discussing this matter the hon. member for Peel said that I had erected four or five roadblocks in the hope that they would be impassable. Well, he did not try very hard to pass them himself, although he did make an effort to skirt around the end. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) accused me of laughing off the idea of a Pacific security

pact. 1 should like to point out for his benefit that I do not recall at any time in this house ever laughing at the idea of a Pacific security pact. It is nothing to laugh at. I do not think any member on this side has laughed at it. It is a very serious question. The fact that we have had nearly
20,000	Canadian soldiers cross the Pacific in the last two and a half years to fight for security means that it is no laughing matter. I hope the hon. member will exonerate me from that charge which he levelled the other night that I had laughed off the idea.
If I may say it with respect, the hon. member, in his comments on this matter, did not deal with the objections which I raised at this time to a Pacific security pact. He produced one argument, and I think one argument only, in favour of a pact. The argument that he advanced, and it is a good argument, was that a pact was necessary at least for the purpose of consultation. The hon. member for Peel also pointed out the value of a Pacific pact at this time for consultation. But I would suggest to him, and to hon. members, that a security pact, to be a security pact, must mean much more than mere consultation. We have lots of consultations now in Washington and in other places about the Pacific. A security pact, if it is to be effective, goes beyond consultation. If consultation under present circumstances would be its great value, and if a Pacific security pact for consultation only would have saved us from some of the alleged embarrassment of the last few weeks in connection with the Formosa decision, why was it that those members of the Pacific region who belong to that kind of pact now, the Anzus pact, did not, by that fact, get any advantage in consultation over the rest of us who do not belong to that group? So far as consultation is concerned, we heard about this decision as soon as they did.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra suggested that we are lapsing back into a policy of a new kind of isolationism, I think he called it-it may have been some other hon. member who used that expression. I believe I am correct in saying that he said we refused consultation because of the fear of commitments.

speechtext:
May I correct the minister?
I was referring to the stand taken by the late Mr. King in the late thirties with regard to the commonwealth of nations, when he said that we could be informed but not consulted.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is quite right. Here
is what the hon. gentleman said, as recorded
External Affairs
at page 1885 of Hansard for February 12, 1953:
That reminds me of the policy of this government before the war under the leadership of the late Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King, when he declared that in so far as the United Kingdom and the other nations of the commonwealth were concerned they could inform Canada of policies but they could not consult us because if Canada were consulted then she might be under some obligation.
Then he went on to say:
We are now having this same problem in reverse. I hope the Canadian government would prefer to be consulted by the United States rather than just informed, as was the case last week.
This action has all the earmarks of Canada being dragged along by the United States, and that situation is not good enough. It does not exist in the North Atlantic area because there we find consultation between members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization . . .
Well, to remove any fears that might exist in the hon. member's mind, I can assure him that we do not reject consultations because of any fear of commitments which may result from the consultations. Indeed, there are lots of consultations going on now, and in practically all of them Canada is participating.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: There was not any about Formosa.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext: He himself mentioned in the course of his speech consultations in regard to the military arrangement for southeast Asia; I think he was quoting from a press dispatch. He asked if Canada was prepared to join the organization referred to in that dispatch. On that subject I can only say, Mr. Speaker, that no such arrangements have been agreed upon. Military talks are going on in regard to an exchange of intelligence and co-operation on military matters in the southeast Asian area. We are informed about those talks, and as they have not been completed as yet they are highly confidential and I cannot say anything more about them at this time.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is Canada taking part in them?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We have attended some of the meetings, and some we have not. We have been informed about the meetings we have not attended.
There are one or two other matters with which I suppose I should deal before I sit down. Many members emphasized, and I referred to this last night, that in any dealings with the United States we should speak up. The hon. member for Peace River mentioned that, as did the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). In reply I can say only that we have spoken up. We do speak up when the circumstances seem to require it, and we will in the future. But I hope that we will

External Affairs
show a sense of responsibility in doing so, and that we will relate our talk, when we have to talk, to our commitments and that we will relate our commitments to our resources. I should like to ask if any of the hon. members opposite would add to those commitments at this time and under the present circumstances?
One result of the new situation which seems to be in the process of being created is that the psychological side of the cold war will assume a greater importance than it has in the past, both in Europe and in Asia. From what we have been learning, it seems fairly clear that it is being stepped up. If it is meant to hearten free men now in slavery and to strengthen their determination to regain their freedom, that is something that we must all support. The essence of that program is contained in the word "liberation".
But I would suggest also, Mr. Speaker, that there is danger to the people behind the iron curtain who are longing to be free, in the misinterpretation and indeed the mishandling of this kind of psychological warfare embodied in the word "liberation". "Liberation" means more than that to those listening to clandestine broadcasts; it means troops marching in to liberate them. We would not be very responsible if, in our psychological warfare, now an important part of the cold war, we gave the impression at this time that troops are likely to be taking that kind of action overnight to liberate them. The trouble about psychological warfare, especially psychological warfare in a coalition of democracies, is that unless we are very careful we will confuse our friends as much as we confuse our foes. Harold Nicolson, who knows a great deal about the conduct of international affairs and the principles which should guide them, said not long ago that we should stop worrying so much about what is in the minds of our foes and make sure that we know what is in our own minds; then we might be more successful. That may be true but it is also helpful to know what is in the mind of the other man. A United States commentator on the air the other night, in talking about psychological warfare, said something that I thought was interesting when he stated: "If we do not know what we have in our own mind, it is reasonable to assume that the enemy can't know and so this might be just as good psychological warfare as if we planned it that way".

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Who said that?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That was said by a United States columnist by the name of Lowell Mellett.

There is one final subject, namely, assistance to underdeveloped areas, which was dealt with by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) and also by the hon. member for Assiniboia. In the few minutes I have left I cannot do justice to this exceedingly important subject. The hon. member for Melfort has, I think, presented an assortment or-and I hope he will not be offended if I call it this-a selection of statistics designed to show that Canada was not doing its part in providing non-military financial aid and technical assistance to other countries. I do not propose to follow him through his numerous calculations but I cannot agree with the conclusions that he drew from them.
For instance, I am surprised that he made such a hard and fast distinction between grants in aid and loans. His attempt to hold to this distinction led him to state that between April, 1947, and March, 1952, the United States spent over a billion dollars on offshore purchases from Canada whereas- and I quote from him-"we contributed not one cent to direct European aid". The fact is, of course, that during this very same period drawings on post-war loans by the United Kingdom and others were considerably in excess of $800 million, even after allowing for certain repayments. The use of these loans during that time represented a heavy demand on our economy. Unlike the United States, we did not have during those years a large balance of payments surplus; in fact we had a substantial deficit with the United States.
Despite that fact and despite the developing needs of our own economy, our contributions to other countries have, I think, compared favourably with those of the United States; and I do not think we need to blush in making the comparisons. As the hon. member himself observed, we provided over $2,414 million worth of assistance between the end of the war and the end of the last fiscal year, when the United States was providing something over $35 billion. Even if the element of military aid in both these figures were to be removed, it would be apparent that we had done more than one-fifteenth as much as the United States. That is a basis of comparison which I think is more than fair in terms of national income. The scale of financial aid that Canada has provided since the war, combined with relatively liberal import policies, seem to me to represent substantial contributions to the economic health and stability of the whole of the free world.
I think it is also important that we should carefully examine priorities between various competing claims. The first priority is, of

course, to provide for our own defence security and the second is the development of our national resources. The countries which we are attempting to assist, and rightly so-the underdeveloped countries-themselves accept that priority. In some of those countries where the standard of living is so low and where the need for assistance is so great, they use up to fifty per cent and sixty per cent of their budget on their own military defence. They accept that priority in spite of their circumstances. I therefore doubt whether we are open to criticism if we have to give our own military defence first priority.
I think it should be remembered also that, with due regard to the importance we attach to economic assistance and technical aid, if war should come the only kind of technical assistance which would be required would be machinery for removing the rubble and the ruin. Yet as the hon. member for Melfort and others have quite rightly emphasized, we must do our part in promoting the welfare of underdeveloped countries. That is why we should continue-and I mentioned this point some days ago-to recognize the Colombo plan and similar activities as being of primary importance in our international economic policy.
This afternoon the question arose as to what we had done for Korean relief. I have not the figures before me but I know that there was a period-and it was not many months ago-when the contribution of Canada to Korean relief was greater than that from any other country, including the United States, and that that United Nations agency at one stage of its existence not so long back depended almost entirely on Canadian funds to keep going. Since that time the United States have made larger contributions than we have; but we have played an active part in that particular field of relief, and I hope we shall continue to do so.

In the course of this discussion which I am now closing we have had disagreements, but more in method than in principle, more in means than in ends. The points that unite us on foreign affairs are far more important than are the comparatively few that divide us. I think we are all agreed on our goals, namely, peace and security with freedom. I think we are all agreed that the threat to us is a global one and that we cannot have any security in the Atlantic without thinking
External Affairs
also about security in the Pacific. We are becoming more and more aware of that fact.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra the other day said that in the North Atlantic council we have been talking about Pacific security. I think that is a healthy development. I think we are also all agreed that the tension remains great and that to meet that situation the maximum amount of unity in the free world is essential.
I think we are also agreed that communist strategy remains constant though communist tactics may shift, and that we should not shift ourselves as their tactics shift but should rather keep our eye on their strategy.
Then finally I think we are all agreed that the policy of building up our strength to be used unprovocatively is working in western Europe, as the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Dinsdale) pointed out last evening; that if there is any easing of the tension there it is because of that fact. We would be well advised to extend to other areas the methods and the principles which we are beginning to find successful in relieving tension in Europe.
In Korea and the Far East, as in other areas where the infection of communist aggression is most virulent, the course we must follow must be dictated by our own strategy and by our own interests, not by the tactics of the aggressor. I think we are all convinced that the fight against the communist infection and its spread cannot be won overnight or be cured by any kind of miracle drug. It can and, I believe, will be won by pursuing a steady and determined policy based on patience, resolution and strength.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I was wondering whether the minister would permit me one question in connection with the Korean situation. Does the United Nations still adhere to the determined policy, as laid down in a resolution of 1950, to unify Korea? If so, have they a policy or plan by which they think that that can be done?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The military objective in Korea as established by the United Nations' resolution is to defeat aggression and only that. The political objectives that have been included in the United Nations' resolutions provide for the freedom and unity of all Korea on a democratic basis. It is of course, I think, the desire of all members of the United Nations that once aggression has been defeated and peace has been restored we should do our best to realize that objective as well.

speechtext: May I direct a question to the minister? In view of the intense propaganda that communist front organizations are carrying on in favour of a cease-fire in Korea, would the minister care to deal with it at a little greater length than he did in his speech?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to do so if the house will give me a minute or two, because this is an important subject. It is the core of the communist propaganda at the present moment, and it may be making more headway than it should. The demand now being made-and we shall hear about it at the United Nations general assembly, I am quite sure-is that we should have a cease-fire at once, and that these other subjects, prisoners of war and all the rest of it, should be left for further negotiation by a United Nations committee.
The best answer to that propaganda is that, if the communist states had accepted that resolution accepted by 54 other states last autumn at the United Nations general assembly, we would have had our cease-fire by now within the ambit of an armistice which would have dealt with prisoners of war. Those prisoners of war would have been exchanged by now, and the political conference which we have been talking about might have begun by now. This new propaganda is an effort on the part of the communists to make people forget that they refused to accept a cease-fire last autumn.
What they suggest now is that we accept a cease-fire at once, with other questions remaining to be determined by a commission of eleven members, of which four would be communist states, North Korea, communist China, Czechoslovakia and the U.S.S.R., and that that commission, which would settle these other questions, should proceed by a two-thirds majority which would give the four communists a veto over any action, or indeed over any decision.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO OPERATIONS OF CONTROL BOARD
speechtext:
That a special committee be appointed to examine into the operations of the government in the field of atomic energy; that the said committee be empowered to sit during the sittings of the house and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the committee; and to report from time to time; that the said


committee consist of Messrs. Bourget, Brooks, Cold-well, Gibson, Green, Kirk (Digby-Yarmouth), Low, McCusker, Mcllraith, Murphy, Murray (Oxford), Pinard, Stuart (Charlotte), Winkler.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving this resolution I do so because I believe that it is the desire of the house generally to examine the government's program in the field of atomic energy. The government shares the view that has been expressed by several hon. members that it is desirable to review this program after a period of three years.
Some three years ago a committee was appointed and did make a comprehensive review of the program and reported to the house on its findings. I think it can be said without fear of contradiction that the report of the committee approved the operation as of that day, and I sincerely hope that another comprehensive review of the program will permit a similar report to be made to the house later in this session.
The program is still dominated by military requirements. Three years ago the committee was formed just after the first atomic explosion had occurred in Russia. Since then two other atomic explosions have occurred in Russia. The United Kingdom has exploded an atomic bomb in Australia. The United States have exploded several bombs in the Pacific, all indicating that the military field is very active indeed. As a matter of fact, it is common knowledge that the United States is spending enormous sums of money, running into billions of dollars, to expand the military program in atomic energy at this time. Therefore our own work in atomic energy is still strictly confined within the rules of secrecy.
We in Canada are not engaged in military development, but the work that we are doing at Chalk River is of importance to military developments, and for that reason, and for other reasons, cannot be made a subject of common knowledge. I am sure that the committee will appreciate that fact and will be governed accordingly.
Much has happened at Chalk River in the intervening three years. When the committee last visited the property the small pile, which was completed in 1945, and was known as the Zeep pile, was in operation, and a new pile of larger capacity was also in operation. The second pile has been doing very excellent work. Its operation has been subject to interruptions from time to time. I think the operation has been interrupted eight times by minor explosions, and today the pile is not in operation. At its inception it was estimated that the life of the pile would be four to five years. The pile has been in operation

for five and a half years, and when the last explosion occurred it was decided that it would be worth while to decontaminate the calandria-the calandria is the interior of the pile-to withdraw the calandria for examination and build and instal a new calandria which would in effect give us a brand new pile for pile No. 2. That would cause interruption of its use for some months, but everyone interested in atomic energy believes that it is well worth while. For the first time we would be able to determine the life of a pile more accurately. We have also determined the operating steps that will prolong the life of the pile. Had we known a few months ago what we know today, the last explosion would not have occurred, and probably other explosions would not have occurred. Therefore we feel that rather than a calamity, the last explosion was perhaps fortunate in that we are able to rebuild the pile and to determine the effects on the pile of the operation of the past five and a half years.
Hon. members also know, as a result of the report of the earlier committee, that a third pile is now under construction. That work is on schedule. The pile will come into production sometime in 1954, as was planned. We believe that it will be the most efficient pile that has ever been built and will incorporate all the information that has been gained at Chalk River as well as information that has been gained elsewhere. The last should be the best, and I have little doubt that the new pile at Chalk River will be the best that has been built up to that time.
In the field of raw materials there has been a good deal of progress. Canada's sole source of supply, when the committee met last year, was the Eldorado mine at Great Bear lake. Since then mining development has been opened up in the Beaverlodge area of Saskatchewan, and an immense amount of work has been done in that area. A mill is under construction, and it is anticipated that mines in this area will be in production by May of this year. The deposit is very much larger than the Great Bear lake deposit, but of a somewhat lower grade. We are certain however that it will make a very valuable contribution to the supply of raw material for atomic energy.
A further development has been the installation of equipment to recover uranium from the gold tailings in South Africa; another development has been the discovery of deposits of uranium ore in Australia. The other sources of supply are producing at about the rate they were when the committee last met.
Committee on Atomic Energy
In the field of isotopes Canada has made a very valuable contribution in many directions. Perhaps the most spectacular isotope application has been the cobalt bomb; at least that has been the most spectacular application. Six of the cobalt bombs are in operation today in Canada and in the United States, and two more will be in operation within a month or two. The demand for the bombs is greater than Canada can supply in any reasonable time. The Canadian pile happens to be the only one that can turn out cobalt 60 within a reasonably short time. We can do it at Chalk River very much quicker than any other pile. The use of isotopes is expanding rapidly in many fields, and their sale has become an important business. The Chalk River organization is on the point of erecting a special building in Ottawa to manufacture isotopes into various commercial applications.
The government has felt that the work of atomic energy should be concentrated under a management independent of the national research council. When the committee last visited Chalk River the property was being managed by the national research council; today it is being managed by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, a crown company formed some months ago. I think this was a constructive step.
The next problem facing those interested in atomic energy is the application of that energy to the production of power. Much progress has been made to that end; but much more needs to be done before we have an efficient application of this kind. In the United States it is common knowledge that an atomic-driven submarine is being developed. We also know that other applications of atomic energy for power are under construction.
Here in Canada we believe that the time has come to undertake the development of atomic power in this country, and discussions are going on as to ways and means of bringing about that development. We feel that the production of power is the concern of those who distribute power, organizations like the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario, or the major privately-owned power companies.
It is hoped that arrangements can be worked out so that the knowledge of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited can be made available to these organizations, and that the organizations themselves can undertake the development work. I am sure the committee will be interested in examining that phase of the subject, and I know the government will

Committee on Atomic Energy be interested in obtaining the views of the committee as to whether that is a sound approach to a very important problem.
We do know that atomic power can be generated at a cost which at present is not as low as hydroelectric power, but which is very interesting, indeed, as applied to remote areas where hydro power is not available. It is my own belief, and that of others who are associated with the problem, that the development of atomic power will lead to lower costs, and a very interesting opportunity to enlarge our national resources in the field of power.
I do not know that I need say more at this time. I might add that all the resources of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, and other crown organizations, will be at the disposal of the committee; and I predict that the members of that committee will have a most interesting experience in following its work.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE INTO OPERATIONS OF CONTROL BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is one debate in which we can all very well agree on the wisdom of the proposal under discussion. The official opposition heartily support the minister's motion to set up this special committee to examine into the operations of the government in the field of atomic energy, and we are grateful to the minister for the information he has given the house today.
As he knows, when the atomic energy control board was first set up in 1946, we took the stand that there should be some committee of the house, or a joint committee of the House and Senate, whose duty would be to keep in touch with the activities of the atomic energy control board. The government did not see fit to accept that suggestion; it was not until the fall session in 1949 that a committee of any sort was set up in the house. As the minister has indicated, there was then appointed a select committee to examine the activities of the atomic energy control board. The motion was worded somewhat differently from the one now before us, but I would imagine that the scope of the present motion will be about the same as that passed in the fall of 1949.
We had advocated that there should be a committee,- partly because of the situation in the United States. I admit at the outset that their legislative process is quite different from ours. But in that country the United States atomic energy commission has, and has had from the start, three Watchdog committees. One is known as the general advisory committee, another as the military liaison committee, and the third as the joint committee on atomic energy, this last named

being a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Representatives.
The general advisory committee is appointed by the president and consists of nine members, all of whom are outstanding men either in the scientific or in the business world. Their duty is to advise the commission on scientific and technical matters relating to materials, production, research and development. I presume in Canada we can get somewhat the same advice from the advisory body connected -with the national research council which consists of leading scientific men from different parts of Canada.
The military liaison committee in the United States has the duty of advising and consulting with the atomic energy commission on all atomic energy matters which it deems to relate to military applications, including the development, manufacture, use and storage of bombs, the allocation of fissionable material for military research, and the control of information relating to the manufacture or utilization of atomic weapons. The first concern there has been the development of the atomic bomb and I suppose there has been far more need for a military liaison committee than would be the case in Canada.
However, there seems to be more reason why Canada should attempt to follow the United States provision for a committee of elected representatives. The purpose of that joint committee, which as I have said is composed of members of the Senate and the House of Representatives, there being nine from each body, is to make continuing studies of the activities of the atomic energy commission and of problems relating to the development, use and control of atomic energy. That is set out in the twelfth semiannual report of the United States atomic energy commission, at page 53. The report goes on to say:
The committee is kept fully and currently informed with respect to the commission's activities. Legislation relating primarily to the commission or to atomic energy matters are referred to the committee.
They are supposed to be acting for congress. It is put very well in one of the reports of the United States atomic energy commission in this way:
The atomic energy act provides for very close relationship between the joint committee-
That is the joint committee of congress.
-and the atomic energy commission. This close relationship recognizes the somewhat unusual nature of the atomic energy program and appears to afford a continuing and thorough-going opportunity for the congress, through the joint committee, to keep informed of and to bring its ideas to bear upon the atomic energy commission program.

The minister has said that in Canada we have followed the practice of appointing a committee to review the program of our atomic energy control board, apparently once every three years. Of course there is a vast difference between an arrangement of that kind and a plan such as the United States is following. I hope that the government will give some further thought to this question because it does seem vital that the House of Commons, and for that matter the Senate, of Canada should be tied in more closely with atomic energy developments in this country.
I put that forward as a suggestion to the minister for consideration as to what the course should be in the future.
I had the privilege of serving on the committee which was set up in 1949. I notice that the same members are to be appointed this year with the exception that the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Murray) replaces the Hon. Louis Breithaupt, who is now the lieutenant-governor of Ontario. I have never served on a committee where the work was more interesting or where there was more co-operation, and I give some credit for that to the chairman, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith). We had worth-while sessions and I am sure that all hon. members who are going back on the new committee are delighted that they are to have that opportunity.
I must say also that I was much impressed by the spirit of the young Canadians who are carrying on this atomic energy work for Canada. I have never encountered such high morale or esprit de corps as we found at Chalk River and Deep River except in the Canadian corps during the late years of the first war. As a matter of fact, the attitude of the young men at Chalk River reminded me very much of the attitude of the young Canadians in those war years.
Those young men and women are doing a grand job for Canada. I am sure that many of them could be earning larger salaries in the United States or other countries, but as one of them expressed it to me, "Oh, this is so exciting I would not leave for anything." I presume the spirit is much the same at the present time. We were also greatly impressed with the attitude of the universities of Canada. They have taken a major share in the development of this atomic energy program and deserve great credit from the Canadian people.
As the minister has said, in 1949 the main interest was the development of atomic energy for defence purposes. At that time its use for civilian purposes was considered to be remote, in fact so remote that, as I remember, the committee did not spend much time in
Committee on Atomic Energy considering that side of the problem. However, it now turns out that atomic energy will be available for power purposes much sooner than had been anticipated. I notice in the report of our own atomic energy control board for the fiscal year 1951-52 there is reference to that fact at page 8 in the following words:
The increasing industrial aspects of this project arising out of the construction of the new reactor and the growing view that large-scale industrial application of atomic energy was closer at hand than had been expected, however, have made it desirable that this project be operated by a separate organization without other responsibilities.
The report then went on to tell of the setting up of a new crown company known as Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. It, by the way, is under the presidency of Dr. C. J. Mackenzie, who was formerly president of the national research council and who certainly deserves a great deal of the credit for the success which Canada has achieved.
I notice, in checking the reports from the United States, that they are now working on a second submarine, and that also they are working on, I think it is called, a "prototype power reactor" for aircraft. I have here the thirteenth semi-annual report of the United States atomic energy commission which was issued just a few days ago. It says:
A contract was entered into for developing a reactor to supply power for a large naval vessel such as an aircraft carrier.
Also:
Work began on a testing facility for prototype nuclear power plants for aircraft.
A press dispatch dated January 29 of this year from New York reads as follows:
Atomic energy to run industrial power plants and light homes is possible within two years-one authority predicts today-if congress and the defence department would permit it.
A big utility company goes him one better and says it may be ready within one year to build an atomic power plant and feed its juice into existing electric lines in the Detroit area.
Dispatches of about the same time indicate that in the United Kingdom they are also preparing to build or are actually building an atomic power plant to produce power for use in industry.
So, I think, our main interest is now in the potentialities of atomic energy in the civilian field, and primarily as a source of power. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that brings parliament even more directly into the picture. As a parliament we are really very deeply and directly involved in this development. I might give some reasons for that submission.

Committee on Atomic Energy
In the first place, in Canada the state or the government has assumed all the responsibility for purchasing the raw material, uranium. For a time the government had all the responsibility also for discovering uranium; but now, I believe, private industry is encouraged to do the mining but the government, through the Eldorado Refining company, purchases all of the uranium. Also, the state is entirely responsible for the manufacture of any products of this uranium and for the distribution of those products. Some day, and I take it from what the minister has said today that the day has just about arrived in Canada, a decision will have to be made as to the extent to which private industry will participate. I doubt very much whether the government can go on indefinitely assuming the whole and complete responsibility.
I notice that the Americans are having the same problem. They moved, some months ago, to further the participation of industry in the atomic energy program. For example, I find in the twelfth semi-annual report of the atomic energy commission, at page 2:
The progress of power reactor development and of studies by industrial teams on possible combinations of plutonium and power production, along with the mounting impact of atomic energy progress upon the industrial community of the nation, led to the establishment of an office of industrial development . . . This office . . . maintains a positive, continous link-up between American industry, large and small, and the atomic energy program for purposes of the widest possible participation of industry in the program, and the widest possible service of the atomic energy program to industry.
This twelfth report also indicates that for the first time industry was being permitted to build one of the reactors. All the rest were built by the commission; apparently permission had been given for one privately owned reactor.
Then in the thirteenth report, the latest report, we find that they really have come up against the problem of what part industry is to play, and on page 3 we find this:
Highly important for the long pull in the nuclear power field, industrial firms and leaders have evinced a solid and a growing interest in power reactor development. This interest was indicated in part by the increasing number of suggestions that the atomic energy act be revised to encourage further industrial activity. These suggestions raise policy issues as atomic energy development enters its second decade.
It is hard for us to realize that it is now over ten, years since atomic energy work first began.
The considerations involved are neither few nor simple. Pages could be filled with the main questions of policy and the smaller questions of detail which follow in their train.

On page 23 we find a further reference to the same problem as follows:
The anticipated large-scale participation by industry raises unique policy and contractual problems on such matters as ownership of plants, licensing and use of fissionable materials, secrecy, patent rights, public safety, and liability in case of disaster. Such broad questions require that decisions be reached in collaboration with other government agencies.
Now, Canada will be faced with those same problems and the responsibility, in the long run, will have to rest on the Canadian parliament.
Then another reason why I say we are directly involved is the cost. The country has to finance this program and, as I read the estimates for the coming fiscal year, there will be nearly $20 million required for the atomic energy control board. The minister can correct me if I am wrong in that, but I think the figure is approximately correct.

Well, the figures are found on page 45 of the estimates, under "National research council and atomic energy control board", and they add up this way: Administration expenses of the atomic energy control board, grants for research, current operation and maintenance of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, construction or acquisition of buildings-a total of $12,466,888. The figures taken together total between $19 and $20 million, and for the fiscal year which is expiring on March 31 the figure is about $17-5 million. In any event, a lot of money is involved and it is the responsibility of parliament to pass those votes and, of course, to see that the money is properly expended.
There is a third reason why parliament is directly involved in this program, and that is the tremendously widespread effect that atomic energy is bound to have on our national economy. Parliament must obtain the knowledge necessary to shape wise policies on this question. This cannot be achieved if none of the members of the house know what is being done. We cannot have wise policies adopted here if members of the house do not have information as to what is taking place. For all these reasons, I repeat that parliament is directly involved. I believe that the committee can be a great help, perhaps not only to those who are taking part in the program but also to other members of parliament.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that atomic energy forms one part, and a very important part, of the fascinating picture of the future Canada which is unfolding before our eyes. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we of the C.C.F. welcome wholeheartedly this motion to establish once again the special committee on atomic energy. When we are dealing with this subject we realize it is a most fascinating field, indeed one that excites the imagination. I think perhaps many of us believe that the day will come when the realities that arise from atomic energy will be even greater than our imaginations might portray.
We are particularly glad to know the extent to which our activities in the field of atomic energy relate to finding ways and means of using its power in peacetime pursuits and in the field of medicine. I suppose the world as a whole will not soon forget that the first inkling we had that atomic energy was with us was in its use for destructive purposes at the end of world war II. We still think of it in terms of the extent to which it might bring wholesale destruction. Yet, Mr. Speaker, there have been other discoveries and other inventions across the years, which men of those days thought would bring the end of the world. Instead, those discoveries and those inventions have led to a higher standard of living and greater pro-
Committee on Atomic Energy ductivity for the good of mankind. I am one of those who believe that if we can keep our heads in respect of international affairs, along the lines suggested in another speech earlier today, we might live to see the day when we can forget the extreme dangers involved in atomic energy and enjoy the untold benefits which it holds for mankind.
I am sure that all of us, as Canadians, are particularly proud of the part Canada has played in the development of atomic energy. We hope that very real progress can be made in the next few years, particularly in relation to power for peacetime industry and in relation to the use of this marvellous discovery to aid the health of mankind.
I listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I find myself in sympathy with a good deal of what he said. There is, of course, one point where we part a bit, and that is when it comes to the question of the relationship between public authority and private enterprise so far as atomic energy is concerned. There are those who will see plausibility in the case he was making, but it does seem to me that atomic energy is so important to the people as a whole that a policy of public control is extremely important. In that connection, we support the position that has been taken by the government thus far. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra that further discussion might be had in the committee as to the relationship between parliament and the executive in connection with this matter, but I do urge that public control of the development of atomic energy be maintained.
There are other thoughts, Mr. Speaker, that one might develop at this time, but I think it is perhaps unnecessary to do so. I may take this opportunity, particularly because my leader happens to be out of the house having had to go and record a broadcast, to say that we are very pleased that he is not only able to be back with us in the house but that he can take his place again on this special committee on atomic energy. He found it of great interest when he was a member four years ago, and I am sure he was able to make a contribution to the discussions of that committee which will be repeated on this occasion.
Having said that, and since my leader is not here to check me for saying what I am now going to say on behalf of those in this group, I want to say that we were most grateful to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for the kind words of welcome he extended to our leader when he was able to return to the house yesterday.
